newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysian agents issue call to avoid Singapore port.
newsitem.headline: Malaysian agents issue call to avoid Singapore port.

text.p: Shipping and forwarding agents in Malaysia's main port on Monday called on exporters and importers to stop using Singapore Port in the latest salvo in the tit-for-tat relationship between the two neighbors.
Malaysia's Port Klang was cheaper to use than Singapore Port and its efficiency had improved with more shipping lines calling there, the agents said.
About half of Malaysia's exports and imports move through Singapore Port, a major factor contributing to Malaysia's current account deficit.
Two-way trade between the two neighbours was worth $34 billion last year.
"I think it's high time Malaysians should boycott the Singapore port," V. Muthiah, president of the Port Klang Shipping Agencies Association, told Reuters.
The Association of Forwarding Agents Port Klang said that while it did not wish to use the word boycott, it was "more nationalistic" for exporters and importers to use local ports.
"I am calling on all members...to convince the exporters and importers to use more Malaysian ports," said Shamsuddin Abdul Rahman, president of the association.
"It is not only more nationalistic but we have all the facilities here," Shamsuddin told Reuters.

Industry officials said it costs 3,125 ringgit ($1,250) to ship a 20-foot box from Port Klang to Europe, while it costs 3,750 ringgit to ship the same container via Singapore. Despite the cost differential, Malaysian shippers have preferred Singapore Port because it delivers a faster turnaround and because Malaysian port infrastructure has only recently been upgraded to a level rivalling Singapore's.

The Malaysian government and port officials have for years tried to persuade Malaysian companies to use local ports, but the latest campaign comes at a particularly low point in the often prickly ties between the two neighbours.

The latest row erupted in March over remarks by Singapore's founding father and former prime minister, Lee Kuan Yew, that Malaysia's southern state of Johor was "notorious for shootings, muggings and car-jackings". Malaysians were incensed.
The remarks were made in January during a libel suit against a Singapore opposition politician and publicised in March.

In a rare move, Lee offered an unreserved apology to Malaysians over the remark. When Kuala Lumpur still seethed, he requested the Singapore High Court to delete the offending words from the court records, which it has done. But a war of words has raged on, with the media splashing out negative news about the other country almost daily.
Malaysian tourism officials this month accused their Singaporean counterparts of conducting a "whispering campaign" to discourage Singaporeans from holidaying in Malaysia.
Singapore's Home Affairs Minister Wong Kan Seng denied any official directive, but noted Singaporeans would only go to a place where they felt welcome.
Malaysians, especially those in Johor state which borders Singapore across a short causeway, have for years grumbled about paying a S$30 ($21) levy to drive into the island state.
The Johor government last month proposed vehicles registered in Singapore pay 20-50 ringgit ($8-$20) to enter the state.

Despite the sullen words, leaders of both countries seem intent on patching things up. Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad has insisted Malaysia wants normal, ties and Singapore's Premier Goh Chok Tong said he is willing to let Kuala Lumpur set the pace for reconciliation.
Singapore is one of Malaysia's largest investors, ploughing in $1.3 billion last year. Malaysia provides Singapore with most of its water. ($1=2.50 ringgit, =1.43 Singapore dollar)
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom 603-201-4813
